questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: scan a line as five iambic feet by fixing its syllable count and locating its stresses
questions.stem: A line from an invented poem reads "The harbour lights came on before the rain." It has ten syllables. Where do its stresses fall, and what foot does that make?

options.text: On har, lights, on, fore, rain: five iambs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one
On the, bour, came, be, the: five trochees, each a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one
options.misconception: reverses the foot, so a line that rises on the beat is read as one that falls

options.text: On five separate groups of three, since the line runs long enough to hold five dactyls in all
options.misconception: expands a two-syllable foot into three and invents a metre the ten syllables cannot carry

options.text: On four groups of three and a closing stress, which is the only way to divide ten syllables into feet
options.misconception: reaches ten syllables by arithmetic and puts the stresses where a count needs them rather than where the words fall

questions.explanation: Scanning has two steps, and the first is counting syllables rather than words. Once the line is fixed at ten syllables, the question is which five of them carry a beat, and on this line the natural weight sits on har, lights, on, fore and rain, which are the even-numbered syllables. A foot that rises on the beat is an iamb, so the line is five iambs, and the fact that the line holds ten syllables is consistent with that but does not establish it. The second option names the same ten syllables correctly and then hands them to the wrong foot, and a reversed foot is a different metre, not a misreading of this one. The last two options both reach a count of ten by a rule about grouping rather than about stress, which is why they produce a foot that no reader would tap out.
questions.hint: Count the syllables first, then ask which of them would be said louder.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate a caesura by counting the syllable it follows
questions.stem: A line from an invented poem reads "He put the letter down, and left it there." Taking the feet as five iambs, where does this line's caesura fall?

options.text: Inside the third foot, just after that foot's stressed syllable, at the comma before and
Inside the first foot, just after its stressed syllable, at the break between He and put
options.misconception: treats the opening of the line as a pause, confusing where a line begins with where it breaks inside

options.text: After the final foot, at the line's end after the word there
options.misconception: calls the line's end-stop a caesura, which by definition happens inside the line rather than after it

options.text: Halfway through the fourth foot, midway through the two-syllable word left
options.misconception: measures the pause in words instead of syllables and so lands mid-foot by guesswork

questions.explanation: A caesura is a break inside a line, and to place one you count syllables rather than words. The feet here run put-the, let-ter, down-and, left-it, there, so the comma after down closes the third foot on its stressed syllable, which is the most audible place a caesura can fall in an English line. The last option is tempting because the word left does straddle a foot boundary, and a word that spans two feet is a real effect, but a straddling word is not a pause. The second option mistakes the line's opening for an internal break, and the third confuses the line ending with a break inside it. Either of those would make the term describe something the line is not doing.
questions.hint: Divide the line into feet first, then ask which foot the comma closes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a syntax that outlasts several line breaks does to the reader
questions.stem: An invented poem runs: "He took the lamp off the hook / and put it on the floor where the draught came in / and left it burning / all night / while the rain came on / and got the window / and he lay there in the dark / letting it". The last three lines are two, one and three syllables. What is the enjambment doing here?

options.text: Holding the syntax open line after line so that the reader's breath, not the line's end, carries the sentence into its final verb
Making the speaker uncertain, since a sentence that will not finish at a line end is a sentence the speaker is losing hold of
options.misconception: reads a syntax that outlasts its line as evidence that the speaker does not know the grammar

options.text: Marking each line as a unit of sense, so that the poem can be read one complete line at a time
options.misconception: states the opposite of what enjambment does, treating the line break as confirmation that a sense has closed

options.text: Adding a caesura at every break, since each unfinished line contributes a pause of its own
options.misconception: counts a line break as an internal pause, which is the difference between a caesura and an enjambment

questions.explanation: Enjambment is what happens when a sentence runs past the end of a line, and its effect is on the reader's timing rather than on the speaker's state of mind. Here the clause begun in the first line is not finished until letting it, six breaks later, so the reader is carried over each line ending by the syntax still in progress, and the shortening of the last three lines arrives as the collapse of that carrying. The second option is the classic misreading: it takes a structural effect and converts it into a claim about a person's confusion, when the reader is quite sure what is happening and is simply behind the line. The fourth confuses a line ending with a break inside a line, which is the caesura's job, and the third claims the opposite effect altogether.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the line break the unfinished syntax is on.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a turn of argument from a change of subject
questions.stem: In an invented poem, lines one to four are all complaint about a gate that will not open. Line five begins "It is only a gate." and the last four lines accept the fact. What has line five done that a change of subject would not have done?

options.text: Turned the poem's argument against the complaint it has been making, so the rest is read as consequence rather than as more complaint
Brought in a second subject, so the poem now treats the gate and the acceptance as two matters in turn
options.misconception: reads the turn as a change of subject rather than a change of stance toward one subject

options.text: Marked a change of speaker, so the lines after it belong to a voice the poem has not used before
options.misconception: assumes a turn changes who is speaking, when the voice and the pronouns are unchanged across it

options.text: Supplied the poem's governing image, so that the word gate now organises the lines that follow it
options.misconception: credits the turn with introducing imagery the first four lines had already been using

questions.explanation: A volta is a change in the argument, and the test of it is that the same subject is now being approached from the other side. The gate is still the gate in line five, so the subject has not changed, but the poem has stopped pressing a complaint and started conceding, and every line after the turn is read against that concession. The second option is the mislabel a reader reaches for by treating any shift as a new topic, and it cannot tell a poem that turns from a poem that changes the subject, which is why the line is written as a concession rather than as an introduction. The third invents a second speaker, and the fourth assigns to the turn a job that the first four lines had already done.
questions.hint: Check whether the subject after the turn is the same one as before it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: read a sonnet's rhyme scheme from its end-words
questions.stem: An invented sonnet's fourteen end-words, in order, are: gate, late, slate, weight, hate, late, slate, weight, stone, pine, door, alone, mine, door. Which description of the rhyme is accurate?

options.text: ABBAABBA in the first eight lines, then CDECDE in the last six, with the rhyme families changing at line nine
ABABABAB throughout, because a sonnet is defined by alternating rhyme from its very first line
options.misconception: treats alternating rhyme as the definition of the form and never checks which end-words actually pair

options.text: ABBAABBA in the first eight, then the same two rhyme families carried over, so the poem closes without new sound
options.misconception: assumes the sestet must reuse the octave's rhymes, which would leave the closing couplet with nothing to do

options.text: AABBCC DDEEFF, because six pairs of adjacent lines is the only arrangement a reader can sound out
options.misconception: reads the end-words in adjacent pairs and mistakes the pairings for the whole scheme

questions.explanation: A rhyme scheme is read by giving each rhyme family one letter and writing that letter beside every line that shares it. Doing that here, gate, weight and hate are one family; late and slate are the other; so the first eight lines come out ABBAABBA, the enclosing pattern. Line nine brings stone, which belongs to alone, so a new letter appears, and the last six lines run CDECDE, which is one of the standard sestet patterns and is also where the turn conventionally falls. The second option would require the first two lines to rhyme with each other and they do not. The third would require the second half to reuse the first half's sounds, and the fourth mistakes the pairs that exist for a scheme built out of pairs.
questions.hint: Give one letter to each rhyme family, then write the letters in order.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a tercet gains from a line repeated in a fixed position
questions.stem: A poem is set in tercets. The last line of the first tercet is "and the road forgave him"; of the second, "and the road forgave her"; of the third, "and the road forgave them". What does that shape do?

options.text: It fixes a repeated line in the same metrical position of each tercet, so the change of pronoun is heard against a rhythm that has stopped changing
It makes each tercet independent, so a reader can take any one of them and lose nothing essential
options.misconception: believes short stanzas divide a poem into separable parts, ignoring the line each one repeats

options.text: It supplies the poem's rhyme scheme, since three-line stanzas can rhyme more evenly than four-line ones
options.misconception: confuses the choice of stanza length with the rhyme scheme, which is a separate decision about sound

options.text: It slows the reading, because a shorter stanza gives the eye more places to pause
options.misconception: attributes the effect to the frequency of breaks, which would be the same in any three-line stanza

questions.explanation: What makes this work is the collision of a fixed place and a changing word. The three last lines occupy the same position in three stanzas of the same length, so the ear expects the same shape and gets the same shape, and the only thing that varies is him, her, them. Because the frame is stable, the pronoun lands as an accumulation rather than as one more line, and the accumulation is the argument. The second option would be true of a poem that genuinely made each tercet stand alone, which this one does not, since the third line only means anything because the first two were said already. The third confuses stanza length with rhyme, and the fourth describes a break count that has nothing to do with what the lines say.
questions.hint: Ask what stays the same between the tercets and what changes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: assign a rhyme scheme to a stanza and say what its shape permits
questions.stem: A quatrain's four lines end in the words stone, bone, alone, tone. Which scheme does that give, and what does the shape allow the stanza to do?

options.text: AABB, since lines one and two rhyme and lines three and four rhyme, so the stanza closes on a settled pair of sounds
ABAB, because any four lines that rhyme at all will be read as alternating rhyme
options.misconception: defaults to the alternating scheme whenever rhyme is present, without checking which lines pair

options.text: ABBA, which is the shape a stanza uses when it means to return to its opening rhyme at the close
options.misconception: imports the enclosing pattern of a sonnet octave into a stanza that plainly rhymes in pairs

options.text: ABCD, because a rhyme family cannot be used twice before a new one must begin
options.misconception: assumes a family retires after two lines, so a second couplet would need fresh letters

questions.explanation: The scheme is found by asking which lines share a sound, not by recognising the stanza's length. Stone rhymes with bone and alone rhymes with tone, so the pairs are lines one and two, and lines three and four, which writes as AABB. That shape lets the stanza split at its midpoint into two statements that answer each other, because the second pair is heard as a reply to the first rather than as a continuation of it, and the ear closes on a rhyme rather than on a suspension. The second option is the most common mislabel, since ABAB is a familiar shape and gets applied without checking. The third borrows a pattern belonging to a larger form, and the fourth invents a quota that rhyme families do not observe.
questions.hint: Ask which lines rhyme with which, before asking how many lines there are.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: work out a rhyme scheme from two invented quatrains
questions.stem: An invented poem runs: "There was a lamp left burning on the stair, / and the water in the bucket had all gone cold; / and the child in the passage said a prayer / and the door that he bolted she had watched grow old. / The floor gave back each step that she took / and the rain went on tapping at the pane / and the boy laid his hand upon the hook / and turned back again, and said nothing." Which account of the rhyme is right?

options.text: ABAB in the first quatrain and CDCD in the second, since stair rhymes with prayer and took rhymes with hook
AABB in both, since a poem that rhymes at all will pair its lines rather than crossing the pairs
options.misconception: pairs the lines because a rhyme is available, and misses that the pairs are crosswise rather than adjacent

options.text: ABBA in the first quatrain and CDCD in the second, since the first quatrain returns to its opening rhyme
options.misconception: reads an enclosing pattern into the first quatrain, where the rhyme is plainly crosswise

options.text: ABCD in both, since each line introduces a rhyme family not used in the lines beside it
options.misconception: gives every line a fresh letter, which would mean that no line rhymes with any other

questions.explanation: The check is to look for pairs, and here the pairs cross. In the first quatrain, stair answers prayer and cold answers old, so the pattern alternates and reads ABAB. In the second, took answers hook and pane answers again, so that quatrain also alternates, but with two fresh families, which makes it CDCD rather than a continuation of the first. Alternation is what keeps both quatrains from settling, so the poem reaches its final line without a closing rhyme, and the last line ends on the word nothing, which is the point. The second option is the habit of reading rhymes as couplets, which would be right here if the pairs were adjacent. The third is right about the second quatrain and wrong about the first, and the fourth describes a poem in which nothing rhymes at all.
questions.hint: Cross out every end-word that rhymes with the line above it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify a slant rhyme by what fails to match in the sound
questions.stem: Two lines in an invented poem end in the words harbour and ardour. What kind of rhyme is that, and what does it give the reader?

options.text: A slant rhyme, since the consonants agree while the vowel sounds do not, so the echo is felt without a full chime
A full rhyme, since both words end in the same consonants and a rhyme is a matter of endings
options.misconception: equates rhyming with a shared final consonant and ignores the vowel that does not match

options.text: A masculine rhyme, since the stress in both words falls on the final syllable
options.misconception: confuses where the stress falls with what rhymes, which is a question of stress and not of sound

options.text: An eye rhyme, since the two words are spelled alike at the end and end alike to the eye
options.misconception: judges the pair by its spelling, though the two endings are not spelled alike either

questions.explanation: A slant rhyme is a near rhyme, and the way to name it is to say exactly which part falls short. Harbour and ardour agree on the r at the end and broadly on the final consonants, but the vowel in the middle is different, so the ear receives a partial chime and not a full one. The result is a promise of rhyme that is not quite kept, and that gap is usable: the reader hears a relation without being able to close it. The second option decides the matter on the consonants alone, which would make every word ending in a consonant a rhyme. The third is answering a different question, since masculine and feminine describe where the stress sits. The fourth is not merely wrong about the words but wrong about the premise, since harbour and ardour do not look alike.
questions.hint: Say the two words aloud and name the part that does not match.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an eye rhyme from an ear rhyme and account for its effect
questions.stem: An invented poem sets two lines ending in the words cough and off. The spellings rhyme on the page; the sounds do not. What is this, and what does it offer the reader?

options.text: An eye rhyme, which rewards the reader who has the spelling in front of them and hints at a sound the ear will never supply
A slant rhyme, since the two words share some of their consonant sounds but not all of them
options.misconception: calls it a near rhyme, which requires the sounds to be heard as related rather than only the spelling

options.text: A caesura, since the two lines each stop at a sound that the next line does not carry over
options.misconception: reads a line ending as a pause inside a line, which is a different placement of the same break

options.text: A consonance, since the repeated letter group is itself a repeated consonant sound
options.misconception: assumes letters and sounds run together, so that the spelling proves a repetition of sound

questions.explanation: The deciding question is which sense receives the rhyme. Cough and off rhyme to the eye, because the letters line up on the page, and they do not rhyme to the ear, because the first ends in a stopped consonant and the second in a breath. Calling that an eye rhyme says the device is working on the reader's visual sense, which is a real effect: the poem looks as though it rhymes, the reader expects the chime, and the ear's refusal of it registers as a slight loss, a held-back beat. The second option would require the two words to be heard as related, and they are not. The third names a break at the wrong place, since these breaks are at the ends of lines rather than inside them, and the fourth assumes that letters and sounds are the same evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rhyme happens in the eye or in the ear.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Locating a volta in a sonnet
questions.learningObjective: locate a sonnet's turn by what changes in the argument
questions.stem: Lines one to eight of an invented sonnet read: "I counted the weeks on the kitchen door / and every week the post was light / and I told myself the letter was not lost / but only mislaid, and would arrive / and I told myself again the next week / and again the week after, and again / until the telling took up more room / than the waiting had." Line nine reads "It was not that she had never written." and the last three lines say that the speaker had known she had not written, and had gone on counting anyway. Where is the volta, and what does it change?

options.text: At line nine, where the poem stops offering explanations and states the fact it has been arguing around for eight lines
At line five, where the second told myself first shows the speaker persuading himself rather than reporting
options.misconception: locates the turn where a repeated formula first appears, confusing a sign of self-persuasion with the poem's change of direction

options.text: At line one, where the counting of weeks sets up the situation the poem will later turn away from
options.misconception: treats the opening as a turn, though a turn is a change of direction and nothing changes at the start

options.text: At line twelve, where the last line names what the speaker had known since the beginning of the poem
options.misconception: puts the turn at the poem's final line, when the final line states a conclusion the turn had already reached

questions.explanation: A volta is found by asking where the poem starts asserting something it had been explaining away. Lines one to eight are all one activity: the counting, and the telling that keeps resetting the count, and even the admission in line seven that the telling has taken more room than the waiting is still given as something the speaker is doing rather than as a conclusion the reader is given. Line nine breaks that by stating a negative fact. The second option is the most plausible error, because a repeated phrase is usually where a poem's anxiety shows, and line five is where a reader who distrusts the speaker would point. But a sign of self-deception is a feature of the octave's stance, not a turn in the argument. The third and fourth confuse the poem's beginning and end with its middle.
questions.hint: Find the first line that asserts rather than explains.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: say what a deliberate break in an established metre does
questions.stem: Every line of an invented poem is ten syllables of iambic pentameter except one: "And the whole of the winter, the whole of it, broke." What does the exception do?

options.text: It puts the weight of the line where the metre breaks, so the extra syllables hold the reader at the point the poem reports a rupture
It shows the poet miscounted and needs trimming to the measure the rest of the poem keeps
options.misconception: reads a purposeful break as an error of counting rather than as the event the poem is marking

options.text: It converts the poem to a different fixed metre, which the remaining lines then follow
options.misconception: assumes one broken line establishes a new metre, when a single break marks a moment rather than a rule

options.text: It has no effect, since readers take in a poem with the eye and do not count syllables as they read
options.misconception: denies that metre is audible, so a disruption in it cannot be said to mark anything

questions.explanation: A metre that holds steady for a run of lines becomes a measure the reader feels without counting, and a single line that will not fit that measure is therefore conspicuous before it is understood. Here the line runs fourteen syllables where the poem has been keeping ten, and the two repetitions of the whole of it put the extra weight where the verse is least able to carry it, so the reading slows exactly where the poem says something broke. That is why a break can be more emphatic than an unbroken line. The second option is the reason a reader assumes a mistake, which is the ordinary response and not a good description of the effect. The third turns one moment into a rule for the rest of the poem, which would defeat the point of the break, and the fourth denies a process that the following lines then restore.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader has been given by the lines that came before.

questions.learningObjective: identify which line of a passage breaks the measure and what it marks
questions.stem: Four lines of an invented poem run: "The letter went into the drawer then / She turned the key and turned it over twice / the light lay on the boards and did not move / and nothing came of all of it, at all, that week, or ever." The first three are ten syllables of regular iambs. What is going on in the fourth?

options.text: The line runs fifteen syllables where the others run ten, and its three commas divide it into four parts, so the reading breaks where the poem says nothing came of it
The line is a trochaic tetrameter, so the poem changes metre at the point it reports failure
options.misconception: names a real foot reversal but calls the line eight syllables, which is not what the line contains

options.text: The line is a normal iambic line with an extra unstressed syllable, which is a common and unremarkable licence
options.misconception: counts the extra syllables but ignores the three pauses, which is where the line does its work

options.text: The line is a scansion error by the poet, and the three preceding lines show the measure that was intended
options.misconception: declares the line a mistake, though the pauses in it are the only pauses in the four lines

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish assonance from consonance by the part of the sound repeated
questions.stem: Two phrases from an invented poem are given: "the wall along the hall" and "six split slates slipped off the sloping slate roof." One is a case of assonance and one of consonance. Which is which?

options.text: The first is assonance and the second is consonance, since one repeats a vowel and the other repeats a consonant cluster
The second is assonance because its s and p sounds repeat, and the first is consonance
options.misconception: names the repeated sounds correctly but attaches each of the two terms to the wrong phrase

options.text: Both are assonance, because each of them repeats a sound across more than one word
options.misconception: collapses the two terms into one, treating any repeated sound as though it were a repeated vowel

options.text: Both are consonance, because consonance covers any repeated sound that falls between two words
options.misconception: widens consonance to include all sound repetition, which leaves no term for the vowels

questions.explanation: The two terms are separated by asking which half of the sound is doing the repeating. In the wall along the hall, the long vowel in wall and hall is echoed in along, and nothing about the consonants is doing any work, so this is assonance. In the second phrase, the cluster at the start of split, slates, slipped, sloping and slate repeats, and no vowel is shared, so this is consonance. The second option is the error of knowing which sounds repeat and then mislabelling them, which is a common and easily corrected slip. The last two options each try to make one term cover everything, and in doing so destroy the pair's usefulness, since the whole point of having two words is to be able to say which part of the sound is being worked on.
questions.hint: Ask whether the repeated sound is a vowel or a consonant.

questions.learningObjective: say what a run of repeated consonants contributes to a line
questions.stem: A line from an invented poem reads "Six split slates slipped off the sloping slate roof." What is the repetition of the sl cluster doing?

options.text: It is consonance, and it puts a hard stopped sound at the start of five words in a row, so the line is felt as hard and sliding before it is understood
It is assonance, since the repeated letters stand for one repeated vowel sound carried through the line
options.misconception: calls a consonant cluster a vowel echo, which mistakes the part of the sound that is repeating

options.text: It is a rhyme, since a repetition of a sound at the front of several words rhymes the line with itself
options.misconception: inflates a pattern inside the line into a rhyme, which is a relation between separate line endings

options.text: It is metric, since five two-syllable words in succession are enough to establish a foot
options.misconception: credits a repeated consonant with setting the feet, which are counted in syllables and not in sound families

The third confuses a pattern running through a line with a rhyme, which is a relation between the ends of separate lines. The fourth guesses at metre from a count of words, and a reader who scanned the line would find a different problem there.

questions.topic: Assonance and consonance distinguished in a passage
questions.learningObjective: name each sound pattern in a passage and say why the difference matters
questions.stem: A stanza runs: "The cold was in the coat and in the hall, / the lamp along the wall had nearly failed, / and all the little children in the yard / had learned to say the yard and call it hard." Which account of the sound is best supported?

options.text: The long vowel in coat, hall, wall, yard and hard is assonance holding the stanza low, and the t, l and d endings are consonance closing every line
Only assonance is present, since the line endings rhyme and rhyme subsumes every other repetition of sound
options.misconception: treats rhyme as a cover for all other sound patterning, so the consonant work goes unnamed

options.text: Only consonance is present, since the repeated t, l and d are harder for a reader to hear than the vowels are
options.misconception: assumes the ear misses consonant patterns, which is why repeated consonants are often used for effect unnoticed

options.text: The patterns are incidental to the sense, since a stanza whose lines rhyme evenly will carry its feeling in the rhyme alone
options.misconception: dismisses the sound work as decorative, which is the belief the passage is written to contradict

The repeated t, l and d sounds are a separate matter: they close off the consonants, so the lines end hard and the stanza cannot quite let go, which is again what the cold is doing. questions.learningObjective: say what a refrain gives a poem structurally
questions.stem: A poem repeats the line "and the sea took the boat" at the end of stanzas one, three, five, seven and nine, and nowhere else. What does the refrain's placement give the reader?

options.text: A fixed interval, so the reader can measure the distance between returns and hear each return as the same moment approached again
A summary, since a line repeated is a line the poem has decided is its central claim
options.misconception: confuses repetition with emphasis, which a single placement can also supply without any interval

options.text: An ending, since the poem's last appearance of the line closes the sequence the earlier ones set up
options.misconception: requires the refrain to land last, though a poem may place it everywhere except at the close

options.text: A refrain in the strict sense, since only a line that returns at regular intervals may properly be called one
options.misconception: makes a technical label into the condition, so that a refrain that is irregular would not count as one

The third assumes the last occurrence must be the ending, which is a rule about a particular kind of poem rather than about refrains. The fourth is a plausible-sounding refinement that would exclude from the term the very irregularities the device is often used for.
questions.hint: Ask how many stanzas separate one return from the next.

questions.stem: A poem's refrain is "and the sea took the boat", ending stanzas one, three, five, seven and nine. The last stanza, the eleventh, ends "and the sea took the boat, and he could not." What has the poem done?

It has replaced the refrain, so the poem's last line no longer follows the pattern the first nine stanzas set up

options.text: It has made the refrain into a new line, and the poem now ends on a sentence rather than on a repeated unit

options.text: It has broken the poem's contract with the reader, which is why the addition reads as an authorial intrusion
options.misconception: calls a patterned ending an intrusion, when the pattern is what licenses the addition

The poem is therefore printed as a widening wedge. What is the arrangement doing?

options.text: It makes the reader's eye travel outward and down at the same time, so the loss the sentences report is something the page performs before it is said
It keeps the poem's lines in a fixed column, so the reader sees a single object rather than a sequence of events
options.misconception: reverses the arrangement, since indenting less each time widens the block rather than fixing it

options.text: It separates the poem's content from its form, so a reader may take the sentences in any order and still get the meaning
options.misconception: makes the arrangement a device for rearranging, when the lines are in a fixed order and the shape is the point

options.text: It is decorative, and a reader who quoted the poem in a list would lose nothing of the meaning it reports
options.misconception: assumes the meaning survives reflow, which is the test that shows whether the shape is load-bearing

The fourth is the useful test, and the poem fails it.

questions.learningObjective: compare a shaped poem's page with its words and account for the difference
questions.stem: A poem prints its lines as a narrowing triangle, the first line longest and each succeeding line shorter by a word, so the block tapers to a single word. Its last word is locked. The sentences report a series of surrenders. What does the taper add that the sentences do not?

The reader is given a shape to remember when the poem is quoted, so the form survives a change of typeface
options.misconception: credits the shape with durability in quotation, which is a property of any printed poem

options.text: The reader is shown that the poem has a fixed order, since the taper cannot be reordered without losing the effect
options.misconception: makes the shape a claim about sequence, when any set of lines has a fixed order to begin with

options.text: The reader can see the argument before reading it, which is what any shape poem claims to offer its readers
options.misconception: reduces the form to advance notice, which would be true of a shape with no content in it at all

The form is therefore a claim about rate and quantity of loss, which the prose cannot make while still being a sequence of events of equal size. questions.topic: Free verse and what it does not mean
questions.learningObjective: state what free verse does and does not claim about line endings
questions.stem: Free verse is verse with no regular metre and no stanza or rhyme structure. Which of these does free verse not mean?

That the poem has no structure of any kind, so that the reader is given nothing to count
options.misconception: treats the absence of metre as the absence of all pattern, which confuses rule with arrangement

options.text: That the poem has no line endings, so that it is best read as one continuous paragraph
options.misconception: assumes the loss of metre means the loss of lines, though a free verse line is a line like any other

options.text: That any arrangement of words on the page counts as a poem, so the form sets no requirement on the writer
options.misconception: draws a licence from the absence of a scheme, which no form of verse has ever granted

Once the metre and the stanza are gone, the only unit left is the decision to end a line here, and that decision becomes the poem's remaining formal instrument, so a line ending in free verse is a claim rather than a habit. That is why a free verse line can be cut short, run long, or stop a clause in an awkward place: each of those is now saying something. The second option is the belief most often attached to the form, and it converts a loosened rule into an absence of rules, which is not what losing one rule does. The third forgets that lines exist, and the fourth is a licence no verse form has ever offered.
questions.hint: Ask which unit survives when metre and stanza are gone.

questions.learningObjective: decide which of two lineations better serves a poem's claim
questions.stem: A poet has written in free verse: "he said it twice and then he said it once more and then he did not say it at all for a year and then one morning in the market he said it again and nobody heard him including me." The poet's note says the line breaks are meant to register each refusal. Which lineation serves that?

options.text: One line for each refusal, ending on a year / on all / and on again, so the breaks fall where the saying stops and starts
One line for each occasion of speaking, so that the reader counts the seven times before counting the silences
options.misconception: measures the claim by occasions of speech, where the note asks for the stops and starts to be audible

options.text: The whole sentence as a single unbroken line, so that no break can be mistaken for a refusal in its own right
options.misconception: removes the device the note asks for, since with one line there are no breaks to register anything

options.text: Lines of equal length throughout, so that the reader hears a regular measure standing in for the metre the poem has given up
options.misconception: restores a regularity that the note's subject, refusals of irregular length, would contradict

questions.explanation: The note asks for a specific thing, and the lineation has to deliver that thing rather than a related one. The fourth imposes a regular measure, and since the silences in this sentence are of very different lengths, a uniform line would contradict the very thing the note describes.

questions.learningObjective: say what makes a passage in prose syntax count as a poem
questions.stem: A passage is printed in unbroken paragraphs with continuous syntax and no line breaks, and it is offered as a poem rather than as an extract of one. What makes it a poem?

options.text: It is set as a poem, and its compression, its attention to sound, and the fact that a reader is expected to read it more than once
It is short, since anything short enough to read at a breath is a poem rather than a piece of prose
options.misconception: makes length the test, which would put every short note and letter into the form

options.text: It is printed on its own page, since a page given to nothing else marks a change of kind
options.misconception: treats the physical page as the qualification, which any excerpt can claim

options.text: It has no paragraph breaks, since a poem's line is the smallest unit and paragraphs are a prose habit
options.misconception: confuses the absence of paragraphs with verse, since a prose poem may well have both

questions.topic: Prose poem identified in a passage
questions.learningObjective: identify the choices that make a prose passage a poem
questions.stem: A printed passage runs: "The house had a smell like a biscuit tin, and the tin was always somewhere, and I have never known where. It was not a good smell. It was the smell of a house that has been shut for two years and then opened, and there is no word for that except that one, and I have looked." It is offered as a poem. Which feature is doing the work of verse?

The length of the sentences, which are long enough to be read aloud and to be felt as periods of speech
options.misconception: credits syntax that is ordinary prose with an effect only verse can have

options.text: The single paragraph, which gives the passage a shape that a reader can hold in one breath and one block
options.misconception: makes a paragraph's shape carry verse's work, which is a layout fact rather than a compression

options.text: The plainness of the words, since a poem is best written without ornament and this passage avoids every figure
options.misconception: takes restraint to be the defining mark, when plain diction is available to any kind of prose

questions.learningObjective: name the conventions an elegy works within
questions.stem: A poem mourning a dead person, with no argument and no plot, follows what appears to be a settled pattern. Which set belongs to that pattern?

options.text: A lament for the dead, praise of what was lost, the naming of an absence, and a turn towards consolation or hope
A question put to the dead person, an answer, and a judgement on the questioner at the end
options.misconception: prescribes a structure the form does not require, since the question may go unanswered and often does

options.text: A death described, a funeral described, and the survivors going home, in that order and no other
options.misconception: reduces the form to a sequence of occasions, which any narrative of a death would also have

options.text: Praise of the living, so that the dead are measured by those who continue after them
options.misconception: inverts the form, since what the elegy praises is the one who is gone rather than those who remain

It laments, it praises, it names what is now missing, and it either arrives at consolation or deliberately refuses to. The fourth reverses the direction of the praise, which is the surest sign that a reader has the form wrong: what the elegy holds up is the one who cannot be praised in person.

questions.stem: An elegy praises its dead subject in six stanzas, then a final stanza says: "and if this is the shape that grief is expected to take, I have kept to it, and the keeping is the part I cannot forgive." What is the last stanza doing?

It is dropping the convention, and the poem now turns into an argument about grief that the first six stanzas were setting up

options.text: It is offering the consolation the convention looks for, and doing so late enough that the reader accepts it at the end

options.text: It is a coda in the musical sense, since an elegy is a setting and this is the passage after the last sung line

questions.learningObjective: say what naming an auditor changes in a lyric
questions.stem: A lyric opens "You left the gate open, and I have not been able to walk through a gate since." Its address is named in the first line rather than implied. What does the named address buy the poem?

A response, since a poem that names its addressee is one that expects to be answered and often is
options.misconception: supposes a reply will follow, when a named address is a position and not a promise of one

options.text: A subject, since naming a listener is how a lyric decides what it is going to be about
options.misconception: confuses the choice of addressee with the choice of subject, which are separate decisions

options.text: A setting, since a named addressee brings a person and a place into the poem with the address
options.misconception: believes a name carries a location, which is a claim about stage directions rather than about a lyric

questions.learningObjective: state what a sestina does with its six end-words
questions.stem: A sestina sets the same six end-words in the same order in every stanza, and rearranges them by a fixed rule from stanza to stanza. What does that rule do?

options.text: It makes the same six words meet in new neighbours, so a reader who has learnt one stanza's sense is forced to rebuild it in the next
It keeps the sense of each stanza constant, since a fixed set of words necessarily carries a fixed meaning
options.misconception: assumes fixed words fix meaning, which is the opposite of what recombination is for

options.text: It slows the reading until the pattern is grasped, after which the poem can be skimmed by pattern alone
options.misconception: reduces the form to a puzzle with a solution, which the rule can be but the poem is not

options.text: It removes the need for a subject, since a form this strict can be carried by its machinery alone
options.misconception: infers that strict form can dispense with content, which is the opposite of what strictness reveals

The word that ended a stanza next to that one may end the next stanza several lines away, and a sense that was carried by two words in a fixed order has to be rebuilt from a different order, so a reader who has settled into stanza two is unsettled in stanza three. questions.learningObjective: apply a sestina's permutation to one stanza's end-words
questions.stem: In a sestina whose first stanza's end-words are A B C D E F in that order, the second stanza's are the same six words in the order 6, 1, 5, 2, 4, 3. What is the second stanza's end-word order?

options.text: F A E B D C, taking the sixth word first, then the first, then the fifth, then the second, then the fourth, then the third
A B C D E F, since a sestina keeps its end-words in one order and changes only the stanza they appear in
options.misconception: holds that a fixed set of words implies a fixed order, which leaves nothing for the form to do

options.text: B A D C F E, taking the second word first and then reversing the order of the remaining four
options.misconception: guesses a plausible-looking swap that the rule does not produce, since the rule never reverses a run

options.text: F A E B C D, taking the last four words in the order they stood rather than in the order the rule gives
options.misconception: keeps the first two positions of the rule and then abandons it, which no stanza of a sestina does

questions.explanation: The rule is given as a set of positions to read the previous stanza in, so the answer is produced by substitution rather than by insight. Taking position six gives F, position one gives A, position five gives E, position two gives B, position four gives D, and position three gives C, which writes FAEBDC. That is a mechanical reading, and a reader who can perform it will be able to perform it for all six stanzas. The second option would make the six stanzas identical, which is not a sestina at all but a poem with the same line ending six times. The third invents a reversal the rule never contains. The fourth is the useful error, since it begins correctly and then abandons the rule, and it is the mistake a reader makes when the pattern feels like a habit rather than a sequence of positions.
questions.hint: Read the rule as a list of positions, then substitute from the previous stanza.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: say what a form's strictness lets a poem argue through
questions.stem: A sestina's rule is unvarying across all six stanzas, and the same six end-words are in the poem from the first line to the last. What is that invariance for?

options.text: It removes the possibility of blaming the words, so whatever changes between stanzas has to be the arrangement, and the poem's claim is about the arrangement
It removes the need for the poet to decide the order, since the rule decides it in advance for every stanza
options.misconception: makes the poet's judgement irrelevant, when the point is that the choice of words was still the poet's

options.text: It allows the poem to end differently from how it began, which the rule guarantees because the last order is unlike the first
options.misconception: describes a property the rule does not grant, since the last stanza is derived from the fifth like the rest

options.text: It means the reader need not read closely, since nothing about the words can surprise anybody at this stage
options.misconception: treats a known constraint as an excuse not to read, which is the opposite of the form's effect

questions.explanation: A form this strict isolates a variable. The six words never change and the reader can hear them changing places, so a poem that gets harder to follow as it goes has not run out of matter but has run out of orders that will hold the words still. The consequence is that the arrangement becomes the claim, and any argument the poem makes about the words has to be made by where they sit. That is why a sestina is often read as a poem about its own constraint. The second option is a straightforward misreading, since the poet chose the words and their first order even though the rule takes over afterwards. The third claims a guarantee the rule does not provide. The fourth is the commonest error, and it reverses what the form does: knowing the words in advance makes a reader watch the order, not stop watching.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader watches in a poem where the words never change.

questions.learningObjective: reconstruct a sestina's stanza sequence from the permutation
questions.stem: The six stanzas of a sestina have been printed in scrambled order as options A to F, where their end-words are: A, F A E B D C; B, C F D A B E; C, E C B F A D; D, A B C D E F; E, B D F E C A; F, D E A C F B. The rule is that each stanza takes the previous stanza's words in the order 6, 1, 5, 2, 4, 3, and the first stanza is the one the rule cannot have produced. Restore the order.

options.text: The stanza whose end-words are A B C D E F, which no stanza can be derived from and which is therefore the first
The stanza whose end-words are C F D A B E, which is the second the rule produces from A B C D E F
The stanza whose end-words are B D F E C A, which is the last of the six
The stanza whose end-words are F A E B D C, which is the first the rule produces from A B C D E F
The stanza whose end-words are E C B F A D, which the rule produces from C F D A B E
The stanza whose end-words are D E A C F B, which the rule produces from E C B F A D

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by one thing: exactly one stanza is the one the rule cannot have produced, and that is the first. A B C D E F gives, in the positions 6, 1, 5, 2, 4, 3, the set F A E B D C, so that set cannot also be first, and A B C D E F is the head of the sequence. Applying the rule to F A E B D C gives C F D A B E, which is the next. Applying it to C F D A B E gives E C B F A D, then to that gives D E A C F B, and to that gives B D F E C A. Each step is a substitution of positions and none of them requires a guess, so the order runs A B C D E F, then F A E B D C, then C F D A B E, then E C B F A D, then D E A C F B, and finally B D F E C A.

questions.learningObjective: state what the two refrains of a villanelle do
questions.stem: A villanelle is nineteen lines long. Two lines are set apart as refrains, one opening the poem and one in the third line, and the two of them alternate at the ends of the lines from the sixth onward. What does that alternation do?

options.text: It makes the poem advance in single steps, since the reader's attention is held by one refrain and then the other, never both at once
It closes the poem on both refrains together, so that the last four lines can be read as the two lines meeting
options.misconception: describes an effect the alternation prevents, since the two refrains never share a line in a villanelle

options.text: It makes the poem's middle predictable, which is why a villanelle is usually read aloud rather than silently
options.misconception: infers a reading practice from formal predictability, which is not a consequence of it

options.text: It lets the poet drop a refrain for a stanza to show that something has changed, since the rule is not a rule
options.misconception: supposes the rule can be suspended, which would leave the reader without the measure it supplies

questions.explanation: Two refrains worked alternately give the reader one thing to hold at a time, and that is what makes a villanelle feel like progress rather than repetition. Between the returns the poem has a whole tercet to move, and the return then measures how far it got, so the alternation is a metronome the content is set against. Nineteen lines, five tercets and a quatrain, and the form's whole discipline lies in not letting the two lines be said together before the last stanza. The second option describes exactly what the form withholds, since the two refrains do not share a line and the ending alternates them to the last. The third is a reading habit dressed as a consequence. The fourth is the assumption a reader is tempted to make when a poem feels like it ought to vary, and giving it up is what costs a villanelle its shape.
questions.hint: Ask how many refrains a reader is asked to hold at the same time.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order of a villanelle's structural moves
questions.stem: Four statements describe the moves of a villanelle. Restore the order in which they occur.

options.text: Four tercets, in which the refrains alternate at the ends of the sixth, ninth, twelfth, and fifteenth lines
The two refrains taken by the last two lines of the quatrain, so that the poem ends on both without ever having joined them
Both refrains given before any other line, one at the head of the poem and one in the third line
The poem closing on a quatrain of four lines rather than a tercet, which is the only structural change in the form

Both refrains must arrive first, at lines one and three, so that the reader has them before the poem starts using them. Then come four tercets, in which the refrains alternate at the ends of lines six, nine, twelve, and fifteen, so the reader's attention is passed back and forth rather than pooled. After that the poem breaks its own stanza shape once and closes on a quatrain, and the last two lines of the quatrain take one refrain each, which is how the form ends on both without ever having said them together. The order cannot be rearranged: a poem cannot alternate refrains it has not stated, and it cannot reach its quatrain before the tercets have run.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader has to know before the refrains can start alternating.

questions.learningObjective: state the stanza shape and metre of the ballad
questions.stem: A traditional ballad stanza has four lines. What shape is it?

options.text: Four lines alternating four beats and three beats, with the second and fourth lines rhyming
Four lines of four beats each, with every line rhyming, since a four-line stanza should carry four rhymes
options.misconception: assumes a stanza has as many rhymes as it has lines, which no such form does

options.text: Four lines of three beats each, since a shorter measure is what makes a ballad singable at length
options.misconception: gives the stanza a uniform short measure, which is not the alternating pattern it has

options.text: Two lines of four beats and two of three, rhyming in pairs, so the stanza closes as two complete units
options.misconception: turns the alternation into adjacent pairing, which is a different metrical arrangement

questions.explanation: The ballad stanza is an eight-and-six pattern with a single rhyme: four beats, three beats, four beats, three beats, and the rhyme on lines two and four. The short lines fall at the ends of the first and second clauses, which is what lets the song be sung and lets a chorus take the second and fourth lines, since those are the ones a listener can join. The first option names that arrangement. The second is the assumption that a four-line stanza should supply four rhymes, which would give a form with no room for a chorus and no reason for the metrical dip. The third makes the whole stanza short and regular, and the fourth pairs the lines rather than alternating them, which changes which line a refrain could occupy.
questions.hint: Ask how many beats each line carries and which lines rhyme.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a ballad stanza's single rhyme does for a sung or chanted text
questions.stem: A poet has written a ballad stanza of four lines where lines one and two rhyme, and lines three and four rhyme, and all four lines are of the same length. Which revision best makes it a ballad stanza?

options.text: Shorten the second and fourth lines by a beat each, and move the rhyme to those two lines, so the stanza alternates and the short lines fall where a chorus would take them
Keep the paired rhymes, since a listener needs the first pair to resolve before the second pair begins
options.misconception: keeps a rhyme arrangement the form does not use, in order to preserve a sequence the form does not require

options.text: Lengthen lines one and three by a beat each, since the ballad's first line is always the longest of the four
options.misconception: inverts the alternation, putting the long lines in the wrong positions

options.text: Add a fifth line, since a ballad stanza with two rhymes needs a line to stand between the pairs
options.misconception: supposes a fifth line would be a correction, when the form's stanza is four lines and never five

The third has the alternation backwards. The fourth adds a line rather than correcting the shape, and a five-line stanza would not be a ballad stanza at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what an ekphrastic poem does with a visual object
questions.stem: An ekphrastic poem takes a visual object as its subject. What does it do?

options.text: It answers a visual object with a verbal one, and the answering may report what the object shows or add what it cannot show at all
It describes a visual object accurately enough that a reader could recognise it, which is the standard the form sets
options.misconception: makes exact recognisability the standard, when the form's interest is what words add

options.text: It praises an artist and an object together, since a made thing is only interesting because someone made it
options.misconception: requires a maker to be named, which an ekphrastic poem need not do at all

options.text: It sets a poem beside a picture so a reader can compare them, which is why the form is usually printed with an image
options.misconception: assumes the form needs a printed picture, when the poem works from a remembered or described object

questions.explanation: The form is a reply, and a reply is not obliged to be a description. An ekphrastic poem puts a made or seen thing into words and then does something with it: it may render what is there, or it may go on to the thought the object provokes, or it may add the occasion, the maker, or the moment of looking, none of which are in the object at all. That freedom is the form's point, and a poem that only listed the object's features would be an inventory. The second option makes a standard the form does not set, and would exclude most of the poems written in it. The third makes a maker necessary, and the fourth assumes the poem cannot work without a picture on the page, which is a printing habit rather than a form.
questions.hint: Ask whether the words could add something the object does not contain.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify what an ekphrastic poem contributes beyond description
questions.stem: An invented poem describes a painted panel: a woman holding a bowl, a hinge, and a window with the shutter half down. It then says: "and she is not looking at the bowl, she is looking past it at whoever is standing where I am standing, which is a thing the panel cannot know, and which I have supplied." What is the last clause doing?

options.text: It marks the poem's own addition as an addition, so the reader can see where description stopped and the poet's conjecture began
It proves the panel was painted for a particular person, which the poem is now claiming as a fact
options.misconception: converts a supposition into a fact, which the words which I have supplied refuse to do

options.text: It explains the hinge, which the description has left unexplained, so the poem is resolving a loose end
options.misconception: redirects the admission to a detail the description did treat, and so loses the point of it

options.text: It apologises for the poem's method, admitting that ekphrasis can only ever describe what it cannot see
options.misconception: reads an admission of method as an apology, when it is the opposite, a claim to the method

questions.explanation: The last clause names what it is doing, which is unusual enough to be the whole point of the passage. The description gives three things that are on the panel, and the fourth thing, the painter's knowledge of a viewer's position, is not on it and cannot be, so the poem supplies it. By saying which I have supplied, the poem draws a border between what the reader is being shown and what is being proposed, and that border is what lets a reader accept the proposal at all. Without it the line would be an assertion the panel contradicts. The second option reads the conjecture as a discovery. The third misdirects the admission onto the hinge, which the description has in fact supplied. The fourth takes a claim of method for a confession of inadequacy, when conceding a limit and claiming a method are opposite things.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the passage is on the panel and which is not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate an unmarked caesura by the clause break inside a line
questions.stem: A line from an invented poem reads "The man who sold the boat had sold it twice." It has ten syllables, five iambic feet, and no punctuation at all. Where is the caesura, and how strong is it?

options.text: After the sixth syllable, at the end of the third foot, where the sentence divides without any mark to announce the division
There is no caesura, since a caesura needs a mark of punctuation inside the line and this line has none
options.misconception: requires a printed mark for a break in the sense, which is not what the term means

options.text: After the fourth syllable, in the middle of the second foot, at the word sold that ends the relative clause
options.misconception: puts the break at a strong word rather than at the end of a foot, and counts the feet wrongly

options.text: After the ninth syllable, between it and twice, where the line's sense catches up with itself
options.misconception: locates the pause at the repetition, which is an effect in the wording and not the break's position

questions.explanation: A caesura is a break in the sense inside a line, and the test is the clause boundary rather than the presence of ink on the page. The relative clause ends at boat, which is the sixth syllable and so the end of the third foot, and the main clause begins there, so the line divides at the strongest place it can. Because nothing on the page marks it, a reader finds the break by finishing the clause, and that makes it an unmarked or weak caesura, which is a different effect from a comma at the same place: the reader discovers the pause rather than being given it. The second option is the belief that a pause must be printed, which would rule out most caesuras. The third stops at a content word and miscounts the foot. The fourth is a real effect of the line, but the repetition is a wording, not a boundary.
questions.hint: Find where the relative clause ends and the main clause begins.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: scan a line and locate its internal break together
questions.stem: An invented line reads "The sea was cold, the rain fell hard all night." It has ten syllables. Where do the stresses fall, and what does the comma after cold do?

options.text: On sea, cold, rain, hard and night, the even-numbered syllables: five iambs, with the comma closing the second foot
On the, was, the, fell and all, the odd-numbered syllables: five trochees, since a rising rhythm read backward is a falling one
options.misconception: puts every stress on an odd syllable, which is the reverse of where the words carry weight

options.text: On sea, cold, rain, hard and night, but the line is a hexameter with the word all as an unstressed final syllable
options.misconception: counts an extra foot out of a feminine ending, so the term and the count both fail

options.text: On sea, cold and rain only, since a metrical foot cannot carry a full content word without thinning it
options.misconception: assumes a foot cannot hold a stressed content word, which is what a foot normally holds

questions.explanation: Scanning and locating a caesura are one operation here, because both are answered by the same division. The line's ten syllables fall into the pairs the-sea, was-cold, the-rain, fell-hard, all-night, and the weight sits on the second member of each pair, so the line is five iambs. The comma after cold falls at the fourth syllable, which is the end of the second foot, so the caesura is a break inside the line at a foot boundary, and the reader hears the line divide exactly where the sentence divides. The second option reads the same ten syllables with the foot reversed, which would put the beat on words like the and all that carry none. The third invents a sixth foot out of a word that is simply the ninth syllable. The fourth denies a foot the capacity it was defined by.
questions.hint: Pair the syllables first, then ask which member of each pair carries the weight.

questions.topic: The underlying beat of iambic pentameter
questions.learningObjective: say what a regular alternation gives a reader without conscious counting
questions.stem: Every line of an invented poem is ten syllables, and each divides into five pairs of a weak syllable and a strong one. What does that unvarying arrangement give a reader?

options.text: A beat that can be felt without counting, so that a line's shape is recognisable even when the words in it have changed completely
A guarantee that the line is a single unit, since five pairs cannot be separated into anything else
options.misconception: treats the foot count as a boundary, when a line can be read across its own feet

options.text: A reason for the poet not to vary the line, since a change of pattern would break the poem's contract with its reader
options.misconception: makes regularity a rule for the writer, when a metre is normally a measure the writer works against

options.text: A measurable speed of reading, so that a line of pentameter takes a fixed time however it is read
options.misconception: infers a fixed reading time, which a line of ten syllables does not impose

Once several lines have kept the same arrangement, a reader no longer has to check the syllable count, and the weak-strong alternation is simply there, so a new line is heard as the same shape holding different words, and that comparison is the reader's without being asked for. The third makes the metre a prohibition, which mistakes a measure for a constraint. The fourth claims a reading speed, which nothing in a ten-syllable line determines.

Which account of the form is best supported?

The critic's claim holds, because the three lines are clauses of one sentence, and free verse need not make its breaks do any work

questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order of a ballad's structural moves
questions.stem: Four statements describe the moves of a traditional ballad. Restore the order in which they occur.

options.text: The last stanza names what the action cost, and closes on a line built to be repeated
The second stanza narrows to one night's action, which is the plot the song is about
The first stanza announces a speaker and a situation, as a transaction the song reports to a listener
The third stanza introduces the turn, usually an arrival or a discovery that changes the night

questions.explanation: The ballad's order is fixed and the reasons for it are practical. The first stanza has to establish the transaction, because a song is heard rather than read and a listener needs to know who is speaking and about what before anything else can land. The second narrows to a single night, which is where the plot begins and where the song's scale keeps it short enough to remember. The third brings in the turn, an arrival or a discovery, since a ballad that introduced nothing new in its middle would have nothing to sing about. The last names the cost and closes on a line that can be taken up by a chorus or a returning listener, which is the form's way of handing the song on. Reordering these breaks the transaction from its consequences, and the consequences from the cost.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain how a turn of argument and a syntax that outlasts it interact
questions.stem: An invented sonnet opens: "I have carried the weight of it to the door / and set it down / and the door / would not open / and the weight / of it / was in my arms / still, because nobody came / to take it / and I could not put it down / and I could not carry it in." The turn is at the fifth line, which begins "and the door". Explain how the line breaks and the turn of argument work on each other here.

answer.exemplar: The turn and the breaks are doing the same work from opposite sides, and the reader can only see that by putting them together. Argumentatively the poem is failing to put the thing down: lines one to four are an attempt, a pause, a failure to open, and a continuation of the failure, and the turn at the fifth line arrives as a narrowing rather than as a new subject, because what the poem turns to is the same problem seen from the other end. Formally the syntax will not close: the preposition of is held over three successive line endings, so a clause that starts in one line is still running in the next, and the reader's breath rather than the line's end is carrying the sentence. Put together, the form enacts what the argument says. A reader who follows the argument is carried past each break by a preposition that will not be satisfied, so the reader arrives at the turn already out of breath, and the fifth line's break makes the reader wait for a subject that the next two lines supply. That is the interaction: the turn would be a mere announcement in continuous prose, and the breaks would be a mere texture in a poem that turned clearly. The answer above says which lines and which word produce each effect, because a general account of turns and enjambment would describe the sonnet and not this one.

questions.explanation: An explanation of this kind has to name both mechanisms before it can say how they interact, because each one on its own is visible and the interaction is not. The turn is a change in the argument, found by asking where the poem stops trying and starts describing the failure, and the enjambment is the refusal of the syntax to close at a line ending, found by asking which clause is still running. What the exemplar does that a general account would not is specify: the preposition of carried across three line endings, the turn at the fifth line, the fact that the fifth line's break withholds its own subject. Naming those is what lets a reader check the reading against the sonnet rather than take it on trust. The temptation in an explanation item of this sort is to say that the poet uses devices effectively, which praises rather than explains, and a reader who has only that cannot go back to the text and find anything.
questions.hint: Find the turn first, then find which clause is still running when the turn happens.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a deliberate metrical break marks in a poem
questions.stem: A poem keeps ten-syllable iambic lines for nine stanzas. In the tenth, one line runs to sixteen syllables: "And it was not the boat, and it was not the money, it was the year, it was the whole of the year." Explain what the break in the measure is doing, and why it cannot be read as a mistake.

answer.exemplar: The break is the poem's punctuation, and the reason it cannot be a mistake is that it is the only one. A metre held for nine stanzas is a promise: it has taught the reader a shape and told them, without ever saying so, that the shape will continue. A line that cannot be fitted into that shape is therefore noticed before it is understood, and the notice is the effect. Here the line runs from ten syllables to sixteen, and the added syllables come in the form of a pair of refusals and a repetition: and it was not the boat, and it was not the money, it was the year. Each refusal adds a foot the established measure cannot hold, so the reading is pushed forward three times, and the reader is carried into it was the whole of the year still trying to fit a shape the content has outgrown. If the break were an error, the following stanzas would have to return to the measure and pretend the ninth had not happened, and a reader who has felt the line widen cannot be asked to unfeel it. The explanation above gives the count, the shape of the addition, and the place where the reader is left, because an account that only said the metre breaks would describe the symptom and not what the break is for.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a disruption has to establish three things: that the measure was established, that the break is not an error, and what the break is doing instead. The first is what makes a break legible at all, so any answer that skips it leaves the reader with a broken line and no reason to have noticed. The second is the part that distinguishes an explanation from a defence: an error is a departure from an intended norm, and the argument here is that the norm was left on purpose, since a single irregularity in a long stretch of regularity is more evidence of design than of carelessness, and the surrounding stanzas confirm it by continuing. The third is where a reader should end up being able to point, in this case at the way the added syllables are shaped into refusals rather than filler. The temptation is to write that the irregularity adds emphasis, which is true and useless, since it does not say which emphasis or produced by what.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader was taught by the nine stanzas before the break.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a sestina's fixed permutation of end-words produces
questions.stem: A sestina uses six end-words and rotates them by the rule 6, 1, 5, 2, 4, 3 from stanza to stanza, for six stanzas and an envoi. Explain what the rotation does to a reader, and why a poet would accept that much repetition.

answer.exemplar: The rotation changes adjacency and nothing else, and that is why it works. Take six words as a set and never introduce a seventh, and the poem's only available movement is to rearrange what is already there, so every stanza is an argument about which of these six things belongs next to which. The rule makes that movement regular enough to be learned and irregular enough never to settle: the reader learns the permutation in the first two stanzas and then cannot predict a sentence, only a pattern. The gain is that the reader must keep the six words in mind across six stanzas, and that memory is what makes the envoi's collection of them land as a sum rather than as a list. The price is the one a poet is paying on purpose, since the end-words cannot be chosen for their line but only for their place, so the writing has to be discovered inside a constraint already fixed. An explanation that only said the form is old would miss both halves: the rotation is not a game the reader wins, it is a condition under which the six words have to keep meaning something new, and the answer above says what the reader tracks, why the pattern is learnable but not predictable, and what the envoi does with what the reader has been carrying.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a fixed form has to cover the constraint and the effect, because a reader who has only one of the two cannot use it. The constraint is the permutation, and it is worth stating precisely, because a common account of the sestina is that the end-words are shuffled, which loses the fact that the shuffle is fixed in advance and learnable. The effect is what the shuffle does to adjacency, and to the reader's memory of six words, and to the envoi that finally gathers them. The argument for the form is then not that it is old or difficult but that it makes the poet write sentences out of words that cannot be chosen for the sentence. The temptation is to explain the form by its history, which tells a reader where it came from and nothing about what it does, which is the thing the question asks for.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule changes from stanza to stanza, and what it leaves fixed.

questions.learningObjective: say which line of a ballad stanza a chorus can take

The second, since it is the first line in the stanza to rhyme with any other line in the stanza

options.text: The first, since a song states its main line before it supplies the rhyme that brings it back

options.text: All four, since every line of a ballad is sung to the same tune and therefore returns

questions.topic: An early volta in a sonnet
questions.learningObjective: locate a turn that falls early rather than at the ninth line
questions.stem: An invented sonnet's lines one to four praise the quiet of a house. Line five reads "and it was quiet because nobody was in it." and lines six to fourteen describe the house empty. Which line is the volta, and what makes it one?

options.text: Line five, since it keeps the poem's subject and reverses the value attached to it, so the four lines of praise are now heard as a description of absence
Line one, since the house's quietness is what the rest of the poem goes on to describe
options.misconception: picks the poem's first assertion, when a turn is by definition a later reversal of it

options.text: Line fourteen, since that is where a sonnet's conclusion is placed by the form's design
options.misconception: goes by position in the form, when a turn is located by what changes in the argument

options.text: Line six, since the description of the empty house is a subject the poem had not been treating before
options.misconception: looks for a change of subject, whereas a reversal of value is not a change of subject

Everything after that line is read in the new light, and the emptiness the poem now describes is the emptiness the first four lines concealed.
