questions.learningObjective: say what a tercet's rhyme pattern makes the stanza do
questions.stem: A poem's tercets rhyme on the pattern ABA: the first line of each tercet rhymes with the third, and the middle line does not rhyme at all. What does that pattern do?

options.text: It makes the middle line the stanza's hinge, since the rhyme is broken there and then returned, so the sense has to turn in the middle to survive it
It makes the first and last lines interchangeable, so the stanza's ending could be moved to the front
options.misconception: assumes a rhyme pair makes two lines interchangeable, ignoring what either of them says

options.text: It means the stanza has one rhyme, which is the requirement a ballad stanza's four lines also meet
options.misconception: equates one rhyme in three lines with a ballad's rhyme arrangement in four, which is a different scheme

options.text: It gives the stanza a closed shape, so no sentence may run across the boundary into the next tercet
options.misconception: infers a limit on enjambment from a rhyme pattern, which is a separate formal decision

questions.explanation: An ABA pattern puts a hole in the middle of the stanza and makes the rhyme into the thing that fills it. The third counts rhymes without counting lines, and a three-line stanza and a four-line stanza with one rhyme are different shapes with different uses. The fourth smuggles a rule about syntax out of a fact about sound, and a tercet can absolutely be run across.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a line break asks of a reader from what a stanza break asks
questions.stem: A poem's sentence runs across four line endings inside a stanza and then stops where the stanza ends. What is the difference between those two kinds of break?

options.text: The line break asks the reader to carry a syntax on; the stanza break is placed where a unit of thought has finished and asks the reader to let one go
The line break is a unit of sense and the stanza break is not, so the stanza is the freer of the two arrangements
options.misconception: reverses the relation, since a stanza break is normally where a sense is completed

options.text: The line break is silent and the stanza break is voiced, since a reader audibly pauses at the end of a stanza
options.misconception: claims an audible pause, where a reader is silent at a stanza end and often continues straight on

options.text: The line break makes units of equal size and the stanza break makes larger ones, so the two differ by scale alone
options.misconception: makes the distinction one of size, which both kinds of break share

questions.learningObjective: check a claim that a poem's line breaks are editorial

That the critic is right, since a reader who ignores the breaks loses only the shape of the page and not any sense
options.misconception: grants that the breaks matter and then says they carry no sense, which the four clause ends contradict

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a rhyme that is only visible does for a reader
questions.stem: A poem sets two lines ending in cough and off, so the pair looks like a rhyme and is not one. Explain what the device does for a reader, and why it is worth an author choosing it rather than leaving the pair to chance.

answer.exemplar: The device puts the rhyme in one sense and withholds it from the other, and the reader experiences the gap between them. Because the spelling aligns on the page, the eye completes the rhyme before the ear reaches it, so a reader arrives at the second line expecting the chime and does not get one. The withheld chime is not simply a disappointment: it is a small held beat at exactly the place the page promised a settlement, and a reader who notices it has been given a second, visual reading of the line that runs against the first. That is what the author buys, and it is a thing an accidental pair of words cannot buy, since the words must be chosen to look like a rhyme and to fail as one. The explanation above says which sense receives the rhyme, what the reader is expecting at the second line, and why the effect depends on a deliberate choice, because an account that stops at the observation that the two words resemble each other describes the device and not what it does to a reader.

questions.explanation: An explanation of this device has to say what the reader receives in each sense and what happens in the interval between them, since the effect lives in the gap and not in either thing alone. The first requirement is naming the two senses explicitly, because the commonest account of a rhyme is entirely auditory and leaves the page out of it. The second is the expectation, since a rhyme the eye predicts and the ear refuses only works if the reader has actually made the prediction. The third is the argument for choosing it, and that is the part most explanations leave out: the words have to be selected so that the spelling matches and the sound does not, which is a constraint on diction and not on accidents of layout. The temptation is to say the device is a joke or a trick, which is a description of the surprise and not of the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye completes before the ear arrives.
